narrative:
The model estimates there’s a 20 % chance you won’t pass your final year, which is above the 10 % threshold the school uses to require extra help. That’s why you’re being asked to take remedial courses.

The prediction is mainly shaped by three things. First, you’ve never failed a class before, and that actually works in your favor—it lowers the risk the model sees. Second, you’ve said you want to go on to higher education, and that ambition also helps push the prediction toward passing. The third factor is a bit more subtle: your guardian isn’t your mother or father, and the model treats that as a small extra risk.

Other details matter less, but they add up. For example, your parents live together and your family relationships are strong, which is good, but your mother’s education level and her job at home, along with the fact you don’t have internet at home, nudge the risk slightly higher. You study less than two hours a week, which is below what most students who pass report, and you’re in a romantic relationship, which the model associates with a small increase in risk.

The next step is straightforward: use the remedial courses to build a steady study routine. Even an extra hour or two each week can make a real difference. Keep your goal of higher education front and center—it’s one of the strongest signals the model sees that you can succeed.
